newsitem.title: CHINA: China expansion of interbank market seen sound.
newsitem.headline: China expansion of interbank market seen sound.

text.p: China's expansion of its yuan interbank market to include city cooperative banks as first-tier trading members was vital if the market was to become a barometer of short-term money supply, analysts said on Monday.

The next step in achieving the government's aim should be the admission of non-banking financial institutions, which had so far been banned from first-tier or direct trading through the exchange's computerised system, the analysts and traders said.

Dozens of urban cooperative banks in Chinese cities had been admitted to the market as first-tier trading members, extending direct trading to major cities, the Shanghai Securities News said on Monday. Previously the first-tier market had been restricted to the provincial level.
The market now had 89 first-tier members able to directly borrow and lend short-term funds through the exchange, it said.
First-tier members include state banks, city cooperative banks and short-term financial centres which are money brokerages run by the central bank.
The addition of first-tier members added liquidity to interbank trading, the analysts said. But the two-tier trading system was a sticking point, they said.
"One major problem for the interbank market has been the two-tier trading," a banker with a state bank said.
"To let non-banking financial institutions trade only on the second-tier market is inconvenient for them and greatly reduces their trading volume," he said.
"In the long run, only if all major financial institutions participate on the same level of trading can the market truly reflect short-term money movements in China," he said.
The market was established in January last year to enable banks and non-banking financial institutions to trade short-term funds within 120 days among themselves.
The market has had an average daily turnover of around 2.5 billion yuan ($302 million) since it was set up, only a fraction of securities trading volume in the same period.
Analysts said barriers preventing rapid expansion included a mixture of money markets on which banks operate, and equity markets with non-banking financial institutions as key players.
Despite a ban on bank money flowing into the equity markets and repeated official crackdown measures, irregularities have been rampant amid poor supervision.
"Irregularities have been so widespread that the central government is reluctant to allow non-banking finance bodies to trade on the interbank market in the short term," a trader said.
"Effective supervisory mechanisms must be set up first."
The technical facilities of non-banking finance institutions lagged far behind banks, limiting their ability to do electronic trading the analysts said.

A total of 27 city cooperative banks from 15 cities had been admitted as first-tier trading members of the interbank market, bringing the number of such members to 89, the Shanghai Securities News said.

The market previously had as first-tier members 11 provincial cooperative banks, 16 state banks and 35 short-term financial centres, which are money brokerages run by the People's Bank, the central bank.
The market also has hundreds of second-tier members which trade through short-term financial centres out of the exchange trading system.
The second-tier members are mainly Chinese securities brokerages, trust firms, financial firms associated with major industrial groups and a number of designated foreign banks.
